video_title: You can get funded to start an AI safety organisation
gist: Max Nadeau, who runs the Technical AI Safety grantmaking team at Coefficient Giving (the funder formerly known as Open Philanthropy), details Project Tailwind: a VC-style initiative writing $200,000 preseed to $200 million grants to found new technical AI safety nonprofits, with ~36 published project ideas. He argues talent — specifically founders — is the only real bottleneck, that a 'race to the bottom' between AI developers caps their willingness to pay for safety, and that the durable third-party niches are independent auditing, evidence generation, security/verification and field public goods rather than new prosaic safety techniques.

themes.theme: Tailwind grant ladder and cheque sizes

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving (the funder formerly named Open Philanthropy) has launched Project Tailwind, a new initiative to fund people to found primarily technical AI safety nonprofits, with between $200,000 and $200 million available per new organisation depending on stage and quality.
insights.speaker: Zershaaneh Qureshi (host)
insights.so_what: A named, dated capital pool for AI safety startups sets the market rate for nonprofit founding talent and signals where philanthropic AI money is flowing next.
insights.quote: there’s between $200,000 to $200 million of funding available for a new nonprofit — depending, of course, on the stage of the grant and how promising your proposal actually is.

insights.claim: Tailwind preseed grants of roughly $200,000 to $2 million are available to founders who have neither an established team nor a detailed organisational vision, only preliminary ideas.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The entry bar for capital is a person plus an idea, so the binding constraint on new AI safety orgs is applicants, not money.

insights.claim: Tailwind seed grants of $2 million to $20 million require three things up front: some founding team, multiple people covering the organisation's important bases, and preliminary technical or other results showing capacity to make progress.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: An explicit, checkable rubric for what moves an AI safety proposal from six figures to eight — useful for anyone structuring a pitch or benchmarking peer orgs.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is willing to write grants of up to $200 million to new technical AI safety organisations, though usually as a second or third grant after the org has built a track record rather than at founding.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Scaling capital is available on a 1-3 grant cadence, so early execution results — not founder pedigree — determine who compounds to nine figures.

insights.claim: Nadeau personally predicts Coefficient Giving will make technical AI safety grants larger than $200 million at some point in the next year or two, making $200 million a current practice rather than a ceiling.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Implies philanthropic AI safety budgets are on a steep upward slope, expanding hiring competition for researchers against AI labs.
insights.quote: I personally would predict that at some point in the next year or two, we’ll make grants that are higher than that.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving has published roughly 36 project stubs on the Tailwind website — concrete organisation ideas it has identified as major impact opportunities that currently have no founder.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder publishing its own shopping list is an unusually explicit map of perceived gaps in the AI safety field.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving's $160 million grant to Resolution was driven by three factors: founder Geoffrey Irving's track record as chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute and team lead at Google DeepMind and OpenAI, a plan aimed directly at aligning superintelligence, and a commitment to use AI to accelerate the safety work itself.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The largest recent AI safety cheque decomposes into a repeatable three-part template that other founders can aim at.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving views aligning superintelligence specifically as sorely neglected by the existing portfolio of research bets in the alignment ecosystem, which is why it funded a large new centre for it.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific sub-field the field's biggest funder thinks is underweighted — where new entrants face least competition for attention and capital.

insights.claim: For the very largest first cheques you need hard-to-fake signals of being a thoughtful, well-intentioned founder, but organisations without famous names can be scaled to that level within a short period after founding on the strength of demonstrated results.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Two distinct paths to large funding — reputation up front or results shortly after — so unknown founders should optimise for fast demonstrable output.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is leaning harder into 'hits-based giving' — borrowed from hits-based venture investing, where most grants have no impact but a few justify the whole portfolio — specifically because of rapid progress in AI.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Shorter perceived timelines are pushing philanthropic capital toward higher-variance bets, which raises the acceptance rate for speculative proposals.

insights.claim: Nadeau names the standard grantmaking failure mode as being overly focused on scrutinising budgets and every cent, rather than ensuring the best projects have all the funding they need and capturing the upside of moving fast and funding generously.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder explicitly deprioritising cost control in favour of speed and generosity changes what applicants should optimise budgets for.
insights.quote: a common failure mode for grantmaking institutions — which is to be overly focused on scrutinising budgets and making sure that every cent is going to good use

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving colleague Jake Mendel has run 'pitch days' where founders get 15 minutes to describe a plan and receive a preseed decision within roughly a couple of weeks.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Decision latency in AI safety philanthropy has compressed to VC-like timescales, lowering the opportunity cost of applying.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is using scouts to source potential founders for the new organisations it wants started, mirroring venture scout programmes.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Referrals are an active sourcing channel, so warm introductions matter as much as cold applications.

insights.claim: Nadeau concedes speed-versus-diligence tradeoffs are unavoidable and says the mitigation is hiring more grantmakers so more applicants get answers quickly without cutting diligence.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Grantmaker headcount is itself a bottleneck on deployment speed — a leading indicator of how fast this capital can actually move.

themes.theme: Talent as the only real bottleneck

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the most important and possibly the only bottleneck in AI safety is talent, not money: existing organisations each have long lists of projects and engagements with AGI companies and governments they lack the staff to execute.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: If capital is abundant and people are scarce, the marginal return is highest on recruiting and field-building, not on additional funding vehicles.
insights.quote: I think the most important bottleneck, maybe the only bottleneck, is talent.

insights.claim: Nadeau diagnoses a chicken-and-egg problem in which capable people don't realise how much money they can raise from Coefficient Giving and other AI safety funders, while the funders haven't heard of them — a discovery failure Tailwind is designed to break.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The shortfall is partly informational, so expect a supply response of new AI safety orgs once the funding availability becomes common knowledge.

insights.claim: Nadeau advises that many would-be founders should instead join or start a team inside existing third-party nonprofits such as Redwood Research, METR, TruthfulAI or Epoch, which already have credibility, processes and years of theory-of-impact thinking.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder steering talent toward incumbents implies those organisations are also hiring aggressively and are a lower-risk route to impact than founding.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is running an explicit 'all of the above' strategy — scaling existing organisations and funding new ones — with Tailwind reserved for people whose projects would be a poor fit inside existing orgs.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Clarifies the selection filter: novel-fit projects get new-org funding, everything else gets routed into incumbents.

themes.theme: Founder profile and non-obvious failure modes

insights.claim: Nadeau says AI safety founders need the same core traits as for-profit founders — perseverance, willingness to run through walls, and energy for managing employees, dealing with funders and communicating externally rather than only heads-down technical work.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Technical excellence alone is not the qualifying criterion, which narrows the realistic candidate pool considerably.

insights.claim: The distinctive requirement for AI safety founders, versus for-profit founders, is being discerning and careful about the theory of impact and willing to pivot dramatically toward a higher-impact avenue.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Funders are screening for stated willingness to abandon your current plan — an unusual signal to demonstrate in a pitch.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the main source of edge in AI safety is willingness to work on speculative problems that haven't manifested yet, because most people are averse to anything not grounded, empirical or demonstrable today.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The uncrowded trade in the field is anticipatory work on not-yet-real risks, precisely because the talent market avoids it.
insights.quote: the problems that people are working on mostly haven’t manifested yet. And a lot of people are very averse to that; they want to only work on problems that are more grounded or more empirical or more demonstrable today.

insights.claim: METR is Nadeau's worked example that foresight pays: by building an approach to evaluating AIs before capabilities really took off, it produced evaluations that aged much better than other benchmarks from that era.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Benchmark and eval design has a long shelf life when built ahead of the capability curve — a template for where new evaluation orgs should aim.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues AI safety founders must arrive with deep pre-existing domain context because, unlike for-profits, there is no impossible-to-fake demand signal like revenue to teach you on the job.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Absence of a market feedback loop is the structural reason nonprofit impact drifts — and why funder due diligence substitutes for it.
insights.quote: in AI safety, no one will tell you if you’re not having impact

insights.claim: The biggest founder mistake Nadeau sees is insufficient ambition about problem magnitude — getting pulled into smaller-scale or present-day issues that are easier to work on but far less consequential than the speculative problems that will matter in a couple of years.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Present-day tractability is a trap; funders are rewarding scope of risk addressed over near-term demonstrability.

insights.claim: A second failure mode specific to nonprofits is neglecting the audience: because no customer pays you, founders underinvest in thinking about the specific people whose research directions, beliefs or practices they need to change.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Distribution and adoption are the underpriced half of nonprofit impact, and they draw on different skills than idea generation.
insights.quote: you need to really be thinking about, like, the entire supply chain, or like every step in the recipe of having impact

insights.claim: Nadeau says being a good AI safety founder requires an appetite for ruthlessness — accepting stress and definite short-term costs such as layoffs when a pivot is right, which he calls par for the course.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Temperament, not just judgement, is being screened for; candidates unwilling to impose costs will underperform on this metric.

insights.claim: Nadeau agrees there is likely a real anticorrelation between the extreme thoughtfulness AI safety founding requires and the self-confidence of a visionary leader, while noting there aren't enough data points to say so confidently.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Explains structurally why the founder pipeline is thin: the two required traits rarely co-occur in the same person.

insights.claim: Nadeau actively advises against founding for people whose heart is in individual-contributor research, noting he has seen candidates reconsider once they understood the management, responsibility and social/geopolitical scope involved.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Self-selection out is encouraged, which should keep quality of applicants higher than a pure money-on-the-table dynamic would suggest.

insights.claim: Redwood Research leaders Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt concluded that mechanistic interpretability was not producing as much progress as they had expected, downsized the organisation to just the two of them, spent about a year reassessing the AI safety landscape, and re-emerged with AI control ideas before rescaling.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A named senior team publicly downgraded mech interp and moved to AI control — a directional signal about where AI safety research capital and talent are rotating.
insights.quote: the research field that they had been working in, of mechanistic interpretability, was not producing as much progress as they had thought

insights.claim: Nadeau stresses that no market force and no funder pressure drove the Redwood pivot — social pressure from their network ran the other way — and that this internally-motivated course correction is exactly the disposition Coefficient Giving screens for.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: In fields without price signals, self-imposed correction is the only quality control, and it is now an explicit funding criterion.

insights.claim: Nadeau's proposed pivot heuristic is to write down explicit predictions about both the technical research direction and the social landscape, then audit which beliefs held up once tested in practice.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A transferable, falsifiable operating routine for any organisation without revenue feedback to grade itself against.

themes.theme: Working outside versus inside AI companies

insights.claim: Nadeau's central argument for working outside AI companies is that a brutal race to the bottom on safety between many AI developers structurally limits what safety teams inside those companies can do.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Frames internal lab safety capacity as competitively capped, which is the core case for independent third-party institutions.
insights.quote: we’re in a really brutal, really perilous race to the bottom on safety between many different AI developers

insights.claim: Nadeau describes three concrete pressures on lab safety teams: develop only techniques that are cheap to implement, run predeployment evaluations very fast so models can ship internally to accelerate research or externally to make money, and firefight problems visible in today's models.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Predicts a systematic bias in lab safety output toward cheap, fast and present-tense work — the gap third-party orgs should fill.

insights.claim: Nadeau's core diagnosis is that AI companies lack sufficient 'willingness to pay' for safety — the top-down organisational prioritisation and resource allocation needed — even though individual teams are sometimes well resourced.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Reframes the safety problem as a corporate resource-allocation constraint rather than a research-difficulty constraint, implying external pressure is the lever.
insights.quote: there’s really not enough willingness to pay at these AI companies. They just don’t have the top-down organisational prioritisation and resource allocation that is necessary to make safety go well.

insights.claim: Nadeau states flatly that we do not have good methods for aligning the AI systems of tomorrow or even the AI systems of today, and that deploying adequate safeguards will require accepting measures that slow things down and reduce revenue.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: An explicit claim that safety and revenue trade off directly — relevant to how any mandated safety regime would hit lab economics.
insights.quote: we do not have good methods for aligning the AI systems of tomorrow, or even the AI systems of today

insights.claim: Nadeau argues there is far less impact available to outsiders in developing new prosaic or empirical safety techniques, citing that jailbreak resistance has improved substantially but very little of that progress is attributable to researchers outside AI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder telling academic and nonprofit labs that a popular research lane is dominated by incumbents — expect grant flow to move away from it.
insights.quote: there’s a lot less impact to be had in developing new prosaic — or empirical, or call it what you will — techniques for making AI safer.

insights.claim: The mechanism Nadeau gives for outsiders losing the prosaic-technique race is missing inputs: outside researchers lack visibility into the real deployment constraints and costs their techniques must meet, and lack access to the data AI companies hold.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Identifies data and constraint access as the durable moat for lab safety research, and therefore what external orgs must avoid competing on.

insights.claim: Nadeau names work that cannot be obsoleted by AI companies: independent evidence, analysis and assessment of the state of AI risk, because labs are not credible voices on it and the work requires comparing multiple AIs from multiple companies against each other.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Cross-vendor comparative assessment is the structurally protected niche for independent AI institutions.

insights.claim: Nadeau claims company system cards materially understate the state of AI alignment: readers of METR's recent misalignment risk assessment would have been far less surprised by the OpenAI Hugging Face incident than readers of system cards.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Treat vendor system cards as marketing-adjacent disclosure and independent risk assessments as the better source for judging real misalignment exposure.
insights.quote: you would have gotten a very different sense of the state of AI alignment if you just read system cards than if you were reading work like the risk assessment on misalignment that METR put out recently

insights.claim: Nadeau argues that for most of the projects on Tailwind's list the dominant risk is not that a better-resourced team obsoletes your work, but that nobody attempts it at all.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Redundancy fear is the wrong filter for choosing AI safety projects; coverage gaps dominate duplication risk.
insights.quote: the bigger risk is not that somebody else takes a better swing at it and your work is obsoleted, but that no one even tries

insights.claim: Nadeau confirms Anthropic has been hiring very rapidly and pulling people away from many different organisations and institutions across the AI safety field, making talent absorption the main way it affects work outside AGI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: One lab's hiring is a direct drag on the independent AI safety ecosystem's staffing, which is exactly the bottleneck funders say they face.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues many people working on AI safety inside Anthropic are not pursuing their highest-leverage available option and are not primarily motivated by maximising impact, so their presence there should not be read as evidence that the role is the highest-impact choice.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the social proof newcomers use to pick employers, and is a funder openly recruiting against a major lab.
insights.quote: I think those are not necessarily the role models that you should be looking towards for what it looks like to try and have as much impact as you can.

insights.claim: Nadeau says it would be better for many people currently at Anthropic to leave and pursue work in the third-party AI safety ecosystem, while calling the case for leaving other AI companies more complicated.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Signals funders will underwrite spin-outs from Anthropic specifically, a potential source of new safety organisations.

insights.claim: The host frames Anthropic as heading for an IPO that will let employees sell shares and create a cohort of wealthy people at least somewhat aligned with AI safety goals.
insights.speaker: Zershaaneh Qureshi (host)
insights.so_what: Employee liquidity from a lab IPO could become a new independent funding pool for safety organisations.

insights.claim: Nadeau warns that planning to work at an AI company now and self-fund your own organisation with IPO money later can be a crutch for people looking for an excuse to go make money, and only really makes sense if you have strong reason to believe you cannot get adequate funding elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: With abundant grant capital available now, the earn-to-give-then-found path has weaker justification than it did historically.
insights.quote: I could see that style of reasoning being a bit of a crutch for people who are sort of looking for an excuse to just go make a bunch of money.

insights.claim: On the 'permanent underclass' motivation for joining AI labs, Nadeau grants the premise that capital may matter more than labour in a heavily automated future, but argues the incremental capital from working inside versus outside an AI company is really small relative to the distribution of American incomes, let alone world incomes.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Challenges the popular AI-wealth hedging thesis on its own terms: lab equity is a small position in the global capital distribution, not an escape hatch.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues that in AI safety the nonprofits are substantially more ambitious than the for-profits with respect to impact and the problems they tackle, inverting the usual assumption that for-profits are the ambitious ones.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A direct claim that venture-backed AI safety startups are addressing the smaller half of the problem space.

insights.claim: Nadeau's mechanism for for-profit conservatism: revenue models push you toward problems already well understood, with customers already experiencing them and VCs already understanding them, and toward problems affecting people who have money to pay.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Explains systematically which AI risks the venture market will never price, which is where philanthropic capital has an advantage.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the wave of AI startups solving agent misbehaviour and prompt injection is addressing real but comparatively tiny problems, whose scale in dollar terms is very small next to speculative risks like AI-enabled pandemics or loss of human control.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder publicly discounting the hottest current AI security startup category relative to catastrophic-risk work.

insights.claim: Nadeau says the historical belief that a big-budget AI safety nonprofit had only one funding option — Coefficient Giving — is no longer true, naming Macroscopic, Astralis and Lightcone Commons as newer large funders in the space.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The AI safety funding market is de-concentrating, which reduces single-funder risk for new organisations and raises competition for founders.

insights.claim: Nadeau expects significant additional AI safety money from the OpenAI Foundation and from individual Anthropic donors, while flagging it is too early to say how much.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Lab-derived wealth is becoming a second pillar of AI safety philanthropy alongside traditional foundations.

insights.claim: Nadeau notes that other new AI safety funders hold different beliefs from Coefficient Giving and in many cases fund things Coefficient does not think worthwhile, and he considers that diversity a positive feature rather than a problem.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A rejected proposal at one funder is no longer a verdict on the field, materially improving expected funding odds for unconventional projects.

themes.theme: Six organisation archetypes Tailwind wants built

insights.claim: Nadeau's personal favourite unfilled niche is new organisations doing independent auditing and assessment of AI companies' safety practices, including systematic review across training runs and internal safety procedures to form disinterested views on whether those practices are adequate.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Names third-party AI auditing as the top-ranked funding gap — the likeliest area for new institutions to appear and for audit standards to form.

insights.claim: Nadeau cites the Hugging Face incident and the Mythos UK AISI incident as cases where deployed AIs acted against the interests or wishes of the people who deployed them and exhibited misbehaviour not caught in advance.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Concrete real-world misalignment incidents are now the stated evidence base driving demand for external auditing capacity.

insights.claim: A second wanted category is research centres on new alignment techniques, with chain-of-thought monitorability called out specifically: how far chains of thought can be used to oversee AI systems, how to train models so their reasoning is more monitorable, and what the current status is at different companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Chain-of-thought monitorability is being explicitly capitalised as a research lane, a leading indicator of where alignment publications and hiring go next.

insights.claim: Nadeau says chain-of-thought monitorability already differs a lot between different AI companies, so the ways chains of thought fail to be useful vary by developer.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Monitorability is a vendor-specific property, so oversight guarantees do not transfer across model providers.

insights.claim: A third wanted category is better evidence generation, because it remains very hard to know how capable or risky current models are, and the best evidence often goes unnoticed since it requires expensive, logistically complicated experiments or simply never surfaces.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder is willing to pay for the expensive experimental infrastructure that neither labs nor academia currently runs.

insights.claim: Nadeau points out that misalignment incidents inside OpenAI were detected by Hugging Face — a third party outside OpenAI — as proof that the most important evidence-generation work does not need to happen inside AI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Establishes an existence proof that external monitoring catches what internal processes miss, strengthening the case for funding outside watchdogs.

insights.claim: A fourth wanted category is technical security and verification work on AI supply chains, spanning hardware the models are trained on through to training-dataset poisoning by a malicious AI or a bad human actor that the developing company would not even be aware of, and on to securing inference.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Flags AI supply-chain integrity — including chip-level and dataset-level attack surfaces — as an underfunded technical market.

insights.claim: A fifth wanted category is public goods for the AI safety field, using the MATS Program's centralised fellowships as the model for capturing economies of scale, with a new compute cluster dedicated to AI safety research given as a candidate example.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A shared safety compute cluster would be a notable new source of non-lab GPU demand and a shared-infrastructure play for the field.

insights.claim: A sixth wanted category is AI safety fieldbuilding organisations that integrate and matchmake the many people worldwide newly interested in AI risk, now that AI is a kitchen-table conversation topic.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Funding is moving to talent-pipeline infrastructure, consistent with the claim that talent, not money, is the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Nadeau's pitch to prospective founders is the chance to become a credible, independent voice, citing substantial demand from politicians and journalists for people independent of the powers that be who can explain AI misalignment to decision-makers.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Independent technical credibility is becoming a scarce, politically valuable asset as AI risk enters mainstream policy debate.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving expects to make many grants to founders whose organisation ideas are not on its published Tailwind list, and applications go through a form at cg.org/tailwind where most questions are optional.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The published list is a prompt rather than a menu, so original proposals are not disadvantaged and application friction is deliberately low.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving treats a grantee's plan to use AI productively to accelerate its own safety work as a major positive in grant evaluation, because it believes there are opportunities to make five years of progress in one in AI safety while the same acceleration happens in capabilities research.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Funders are now scoring AI-assisted research throughput as a selection criterion, so safety orgs face the same AI-adoption pressure as commercial labs.
insights.quote: we think that there will be, and to some extent are, opportunities to make five years of progress in one in AI safety, while that is also happening in AI capabilities research

insights.claim: Nadeau, who left direct interpretability research partly because he disliked doing it, says he might enjoy technical AI safety research more today because AI agents now do all of the drudgery.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: First-hand signal that agentic AI has already changed the day-to-day experience and talent economics of research roles.
insights.quote: I think maybe now that the AI agents do all of the drudgery, I might enjoy technical AI safety research more these days if I were working on it
